segments.speaker: John
segments.text: In Deep Reinforcement Learning Methods, today’s lecture is on “Trust the Critic More.” Recent work such as “Group-in-Group Policy Optimization for L-L-M Agent Training” and “G-R-P-O is Secretly a Process Reward Model” reflects a broader shift toward finer credit assignment for long reasoning tasks. This paper, by researchers at Stanford, takes another route: use a learned critic to score partial responses, but only when the critic seems trustworthy. Yes, Noah?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Hi Professor, why does assigning one score to an entire proof cause such a problem?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Because a verifier’s final score can hide where the reasoning succeeded or failed. Imagine a long proof that is sound until one mistaken step near the end: a single low terminal reward can penalize all the useful work before it. Standard G-R-P-O applies the same advantage across a response, which is simple but coarse. The paper asks whether a critic can estimate progress mid-response, so policy updates need not always wait for a complete proof.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The central proposal is Actor-Critic with Action Chunking, or A-C-two. Instead of treating the critic only as a baseline, the method can use its estimate of eventual verifier reward as the score for a partial continuation. That score becomes a learning signal for the generated chunk. The key qualification is in the title: the method does not assume the critic is reliable everywhere; it first checks whether each problem is ready for critic-based updates.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Quick question: what exactly does the method score, the replayed prefix or the new continuation?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: It scores the new continuation. A prefix is sampled from an earlier trajectory, then the policy generates a group of continuations from that starting point. Each continuation receives an endpoint value: a verifier score if it finishes the proof, or a critic estimate if it stops partway through. The group’s mean endpoint value estimates the prefix’s value and also serves as a training target for the critic.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: For each continuation, A-C-two subtracts the group mean from that continuation’s endpoint value to form its advantage. That same advantage trains the generated tokens in the chunk, while the replayed prefix itself gets no policy loss. The actor and critic share model parameters but have separate optimization states and learning rates. The critic is prompted to predict a proof score on a discrete scale from 0 to 1, in steps of 0.1.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: So you’re saying the critic can replace the final verifier score, but only after it passes a readiness check?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: That’s right, and readiness is problem-specific. Initially, every problem is unready, so continuations run to completion and their verifier outcomes help measure critic error. A problem becomes ready only after recent errors meet a global threshold, its latest error meets a stricter local threshold, and the policy has produced at least one correct solution. Once ready, it stays ready. This cautious gate is one of the method’s central design choices.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: For ready problems, most continuations can stop at action chunks of up to 10,000 new tokens, even though the overall response budget is 50,000. The main setup still runs full responses on one quarter of ready problems; the authors call this auditing. Those outcomes let them continue checking critic accuracy. When available, a previous strong solution is also shown to the critic, helping it judge the potential of a partial proof without giving that solution to the policy.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: How much computation does chunking save, and what do the reported numbers actually include?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: On mean validation score, A-C-two reached G-R-P-O’s peak of 18.5% using about 0.79 times 10 to the 20 decoding flops, compared with 1.99 times 10 to the 20 for G-R-P-O. That is a 2.5-fold reduction in the reported decoding measure. A-C-two also reached that score in about 90 training steps, rather than 120, and peaked at 20.57%. Decoding flops exclude training, critic inference, judging, and validation costs.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The comparison with Prefix G-R-P-O matters because it also starts from replayed prefixes, but uses full continuations and terminal rewards. It performed worse than A-C-two, suggesting replay alone does not explain the gain. The authors also found that group-mean endpoint values were more accurate targets than the critic’s predictions at the prefix in one diagnostic. Still, critic-based and terminal-reward advantages were only partly aligned, so estimated progress is not identical to observed outcome.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Could the readiness procedure itself make the approach difficult to use in a new or data-limited setting?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Yes. Readiness depends on repeated full rollouts to compare critic estimates with terminal rewards, and the experiments repeatedly revisit training problems. That makes the current procedure harder to apply when data or repeated feedback is scarce. Results also come from one model, mathematical proof training, and a 60-problem benchmark scored by a separate model judge. So the evidence supports this setting, but does not establish transfer to other tasks or reward systems.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The broader contribution is a change in how we think about critic use: not simply trust or distrust it globally, but decide where it is calibrated enough to influence policy learning. That complements credit-assignment work such as G-R-P-O’s prefix-based signal, while A-C-two explicitly estimates values for partial continuations. The practical question for future research is how to maintain that local calibration without requiring so many terminal outcomes.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: How should researchers interpret the compute advantage if the reported metric leaves out critic and training costs?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: As a meaningful but incomplete result. Decoding cost is important for long generations, and the paper reports that it tracks G-P-U hours in its main run, but it is not a full end-to-end accounting. Nor is the best-of-16 ceiling clearly higher: that evaluation plateaus at roughly similar levels for A-C-two and G-R-P-O. The strongest claim is narrower: selective critic-based updates can reach a given mean score with fewer decoding resources in this mathematical setting.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The takeaway is that a critic can do more than subtract a baseline when its reliability is tested problem by problem. A-C-two uses partial continuations, replayed reasoning states, and ongoing audits to turn that possibility into a training method, while its limitations keep the claim appropriately bounded. For long proofs, the useful question may be not whether to trust a critic everywhere, but when its estimate is good enough to act on. Thanks for listening.
